faqs.question: What product categories does Panjit offer?
faqs.answer: Panjit offers four main product categories: (1) Schottky Diodes - Low forward voltage drop rectifiers ideal for high-efficiency power supplies, DC-DC converters, and freewheeling applications with voltage ratings from 20V to 200V; (2) Fast Recovery Diodes - Ultra-fast switching rectifiers designed for high-frequency applications including SMPS, inverters, and welding equipment with reverse recovery times from 25ns to 100ns; (3) Bridge Rectifiers - Full-wave rectification modules for AC-DC power conversion in industrial and consumer applications with current ratings from 0.5A to 50A; (4) Protection Devices - TVS diodes and transient voltage suppressors for circuit protection against ESD and surge events with power ratings from 400W to 5000W.

faqs.question: How do I select the right Panjit diode for my application?
faqs.answer: Selecting the right Panjit diode involves several key considerations: (1) Voltage rating - choose reverse voltage (VRRM) at least 1.5-2x your maximum operating voltage to ensure reliable operation under transient conditions; (2) Current rating - select average forward current (IF(AV)) based on load requirements with 30-50% margin for temperature derating; (3) Switching speed - use Schottky diodes for high-frequency applications above 100kHz due to negligible reverse recovery, fast recovery diodes for medium frequency 20-100kHz, and standard rectifiers for line frequency applications; (4) Forward voltage - lower VF means better efficiency, critical for battery-powered and low-voltage applications; (5) Package selection - consider thermal requirements and PCB space constraints, with SMA/SMB for compact designs and TO-220/TO-247 for high power applications.
faqs.decisionGuide: Use the parameter tables in each category page to compare specifications, or contact our FAE team for personalized selection recommendations based on your specific voltage, current, and switching frequency requirements.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Schottky and Fast Recovery diodes?
faqs.answer: Schottky and Fast Recovery diodes serve different application needs based on their fundamental construction: Schottky diodes use metal-semiconductor junction providing several advantages: (1) Lower forward voltage drop (0.3-0.5V vs 0.8-1.2V) resulting in better efficiency and reduced heat generation; (2) Faster switching with negligible reverse recovery time, making them ideal for high-frequency applications above 100kHz; (3) Lower switching losses which reduces EMI and simplifies filter design; (4) Trade-off is higher leakage current and limited voltage rating typically below 200V. Fast Recovery diodes use PN junction with optimized lifetime control: (1) Higher voltage ratings up to 1200V suitable for high-voltage power supplies; (2) Lower leakage current providing better high-temperature performance; (3) Reverse recovery time of 25-100ns suitable for medium frequency switching; (4) Better high-temperature reliability for industrial applications.
faqs.decisionGuide: For high-frequency, low-voltage applications below 100V, choose Schottky diodes. For high-voltage power supplies above 100V, choose Fast Recovery diodes. Contact us if you need help determining the best technology for your specific design.

selectionGuide.description: Learn about key parameters and selection criteria for choosing the right Schottky diode for your power supply or rectification application

faqs.question: What are the key parameters for selecting Schottky diodes?
faqs.answer: Key parameters for Schottky diode selection include: (1) Reverse Voltage (VRRM) - maximum reverse voltage the diode can withstand, typically select 1.5-2x the maximum operating voltage for safety margin; (2) Average Forward Current (IF(AV)) - continuous current rating based on load requirements with thermal considerations, usually derate by 30-50% for high temperature operation; (3) Forward Voltage (VFM) - voltage drop at rated current, lower values mean better efficiency especially important for battery-powered devices; (4) Reverse Leakage Current (IR) - current at maximum reverse voltage, increases significantly with temperature; (5) Thermal Resistance - junction-to-case and junction-to-ambient for thermal design calculations. Our product table shows these parameters to help you select the optimal device.
faqs.decisionGuide: Use the parameter table to compare specifications. Consider both electrical and thermal requirements for your application. Contact our FAE for thermal modeling assistance.

faqs.question: How do I interpret the forward voltage in the parameter table?
faqs.answer: Forward voltage (VFM or VF) is the voltage drop across the diode when conducting forward current. For Schottky diodes, this is typically 0.3-0.5V compared to 0.8-1.2V for standard PN junction diodes. In the parameter table, VFM is specified at a specific current (e.g., 0.5V @ 5A). Lower forward voltage means: (1) Lower conduction losses - important for efficiency in power supplies, reducing heat generation; (2) Less heat generation - reduces cooling requirements and improves reliability; (3) Better performance in low-voltage applications - critical for battery-powered devices where every millivolt counts. However, lower VF often comes with higher reverse leakage current, so consider the trade-off for your specific application requirements.
faqs.decisionGuide: Choose the lowest VF that meets your reverse voltage and leakage requirements for optimal efficiency. For high-temperature applications, also consider how VF increases with temperature.

faqs.question: What package should I choose for my Schottky diode application?
faqs.answer: Package selection depends on power dissipation and thermal requirements: (1) SMA (DO-214AC) - suitable for 1-2A applications, compact size ideal for space-constrained consumer electronics; (2) SMB (DO-214AA) - suitable for 2-5A applications, good balance of size and thermal performance with reasonable copper area; (3) SMC (DO-214AB) - suitable for 3-8A applications, better thermal capability for higher power; (4) TO-220AC/AB - suitable for 10-30A high-power applications, requires heat sinking but easy to mount; (5) TO-247 - suitable for highest power 30A+ applications, superior thermal performance. Calculate power dissipation as P = IF × VFM, then check junction temperature using Tj = Ta + (P × RthJA). Ensure Tj stays below maximum rating (typically 125-175°C) with adequate margin.
faqs.decisionGuide: Calculate thermal requirements and choose a package with adequate heat dissipation capability. Contact our FAE for thermal design assistance and package recommendations.

faqs.question: What is the difference between SK54 and SK104 Schottky diodes?
faqs.answer: The SK54 and SK104 are popular Schottky diodes with different current capabilities: SK54 (5A, 40V) features forward voltage of 0.55V @ 5A, suitable for low-voltage applications up to 40V, commonly used in 5V and 12V power supplies with SMB package. SK104 (10A, 40V) features forward voltage of 0.55V @ 10A, higher current capability for more demanding applications, used in higher power DC-DC converters and motor drives. Both feature low forward voltage for high efficiency, fast switching for high-frequency operation, and SMB package for good thermal performance. Choose SK54 for 5A applications and SK104 for 10A applications requiring higher current capability. The SK104 provides better margin and cooler operation when used below 7A continuous.
faqs.decisionGuide: Select SK54 for 5A applications and SK104 for 10A applications. SK104 provides better headroom when operating at 6-8A range for improved reliability.

faqs.question: Can Schottky diodes be used in parallel for higher current?
faqs.answer: Yes, Schottky diodes can be paralleled for higher current capability, but current sharing must be carefully considered: (1) Forward voltage matching - use diodes from the same production lot for similar VF characteristics, as even small differences can cause significant current imbalance; (2) Thermal coupling - mount diodes close together on the same heat sink to maintain similar temperatures, as VF decreases with temperature; (3) Individual current limiting - consider small series resistors (0.01-0.1 ohm) to improve current sharing at the cost of some efficiency; (4) Layout symmetry - ensure equal trace lengths and impedances to each diode for balanced current distribution. Without proper matching, one diode may carry more current and overheat. For best results, use a single higher-current diode if available (e.g., one SK104 instead of two SK54s) to avoid current sharing issues.
faqs.decisionGuide: For parallel configurations, use matched diodes from the same lot and ensure good thermal coupling. Consider using a single higher-current device for simplicity and reliability.

faqs.question: What are typical applications for Schottky diodes in power supplies?
faqs.answer: Schottky diodes are widely used in power supply applications due to their low forward voltage and fast switching: (1) Output rectification - in secondary side of switching power supplies, low VF improves efficiency especially important for low-voltage outputs; (2) Freewheeling diodes - across inductors in buck converters, fast switching reduces losses and allows higher operating frequencies; (3) OR-ing diodes - for redundant power supplies, low VF minimizes voltage drop and power loss; (4) Reverse polarity protection - in battery and DC input circuits, simple and effective protection; (5) Clamp diodes - in flyback converters to protect switching transistors from voltage spikes. The fast switching and low forward voltage make Schottky diodes ideal for high-frequency switching power supplies (100kHz+) where switching losses dominate. For each application, select voltage and current ratings with appropriate margins.
faqs.decisionGuide: Identify your specific power supply application and select Schottky diodes based on voltage, current, and switching frequency requirements. Contact our FAE for application-specific recommendations.

selectionGuide.title: How to Select Fast Recovery Diodes
selectionGuide.description: Learn about reverse recovery time and selection criteria for high-frequency applications

faqs.question: What is reverse recovery time and why is it important?
faqs.answer: Reverse recovery time (trr) is the time required for a diode to switch from forward conducting state to reverse blocking state. When a diode switches off, stored charge must be removed before it can block reverse voltage. This recovery process creates a reverse current spike that causes switching losses and EMI. Shorter recovery times mean: (1) Lower switching losses - critical for high-frequency operation above 100kHz; (2) Reduced EMI - less noise generated during switching transitions; (3) Higher efficiency - less power wasted during switching; (4) Smaller magnetic components - higher frequency allows smaller transformers and inductors. For applications below 20kHz, standard recovery diodes are sufficient. For 20-100kHz, fast recovery (75ns) is recommended. For 100-500kHz, ultra-fast (50ns) or hyperfast (40ns) diodes are required.
faqs.decisionGuide: Select recovery time based on your switching frequency. Faster recovery costs more but enables higher frequency operation.

faqs.question: How do I calculate switching losses in fast recovery diodes?
faqs.answer: Switching losses in fast recovery diodes can be estimated using: Psw = 0.5 × VR × IRRM × trr × fsw, where VR is reverse voltage, IRRM is peak reverse recovery current, trr is reverse recovery time, and fsw is switching frequency. For example, a diode with 100ns trr switching 300V at 100kHz might have switching losses of 1-2W. To minimize losses: (1) Select diodes with shortest trr for your frequency; (2) Use soft recovery diodes to reduce IRRM; (3) Implement snubber circuits to control switching; (4) Consider SiC Schottky diodes for highest frequency applications. At frequencies above 100kHz, switching losses often exceed conduction losses, making diode selection critical for thermal design.
faqs.decisionGuide: Calculate switching losses for your application. If losses are excessive, consider faster diodes or soft switching topologies.

faqs.question: What is the difference between fast, ultra-fast, and hyperfast recovery?
faqs.answer: The classification refers to reverse recovery time ranges: Fast Recovery: 75-150ns trr, suitable for switching frequencies up to 100kHz, commonly used in general-purpose power supplies and motor drives. Ultra-Fast Recovery: 50-75ns trr, suitable for frequencies up to 200kHz, used in high-density power supplies and PFC circuits. Hyperfast Recovery: 25-50ns trr, suitable for frequencies up to 500kHz or higher, used in high-frequency resonant converters and EV chargers. The faster the recovery, the lower the switching losses but typically higher cost. Soft recovery characteristics (gradual current transition) are preferred over snappy recovery (abrupt transition) as they generate less EMI and voltage overshoot.
faqs.decisionGuide: Match recovery speed to your switching frequency. Use fast for <100kHz, ultra-fast for 100-200kHz, hyperfast for >200kHz.

faqs.question: Can I use fast recovery diodes in bridge rectifier applications?
faqs.answer: Fast recovery diodes are generally not needed for bridge rectifier applications at line frequency (50/60Hz) because switching losses are negligible at these frequencies. Standard recovery diodes are sufficient and more cost-effective for line-frequency rectification. However, fast recovery diodes are beneficial in: (1) High-frequency inverter output rectification; (2) Secondary side rectification in high-frequency transformers; (3) Freewheeling diodes in high-frequency switching circuits; (4) PFC boost diode applications. For bridge rectifiers on the AC input side, use standard bridge rectifiers. For output rectification in switching supplies, use Schottky (low voltage) or fast recovery (high voltage) depending on voltage requirements.
faqs.decisionGuide: Use standard rectifiers for line frequency bridges. Use fast recovery for high-frequency secondary rectification.

faqs.question: What causes diode snappy recovery and how can I prevent it?
faqs.answer: Snappy recovery occurs when a diode turns off abruptly, causing high di/dt and voltage overshoot due to circuit inductance. This can damage the diode and generate excessive EMI. Causes include: (1) High circuit inductance in the commutation loop; (2) Fast switching transistors driving the diode; (3) Diodes with abrupt recovery characteristics. Prevention methods: (1) Use soft recovery diodes designed for gradual current transition; (2) Minimize loop inductance with tight PCB layout; (3) Add RC snubbers across the diode to dampen voltage spikes; (4) Use saturable reactors or small inductors to slow current transitions; (5) Select diodes with specified soft recovery characteristics. Panjit's fast recovery diodes feature soft recovery design to minimize snappy behavior.
faqs.decisionGuide: Use soft recovery diodes and minimize loop inductance. Add snubbers if voltage overshoot is observed.

faqs.question: How do I select the voltage rating for fast recovery diodes?
faqs.answer: Voltage rating selection for fast recovery diodes follows similar principles to other diodes: VRRM should be at least 1.5-2x the maximum reverse voltage seen in the application. For PFC circuits, consider the peak output voltage plus margin. For inverter applications, consider DC bus voltage plus switching transients. Key considerations: (1) High-voltage applications (>600V) require fast recovery diodes as Schottky diodes are limited to ~200V; (2) Higher voltage diodes typically have longer recovery times - select the lowest voltage rating that meets your needs; (3) Temperature derating - maximum voltage decreases at high temperatures; (4) Safety standards may require specific voltage margins. Panjit offers fast recovery diodes from 600V to 1200V to cover most high-voltage power supply applications.
faqs.decisionGuide: Select VRRM at least 1.5x maximum operating voltage. Use lowest voltage rating that meets requirements for best performance.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the power dissipation in a bridge rectifier?
faqs.answer: Power dissipation in a bridge rectifier is calculated as P = 2 × VF × Idc, where VF is forward voltage drop per diode and Idc is DC output current. The factor of 2 accounts for two diodes conducting simultaneously in a full-wave bridge. For example, with 1V forward drop and 5A output: P = 2 × 1V × 5A = 10W. Thermal considerations: (1) Junction temperature Tj = Ta + (P × RthJA); (2) Must keep Tj below maximum rating (typically 150°C); (3) Heat sinking required for currents above 2-3A; (4) Bridge rectifiers run hot - ensure adequate cooling. For high-current applications, consider Schottky bridges (lower VF) or chassis-mount packages with heat sinks.
faqs.decisionGuide: Calculate power dissipation and ensure adequate thermal management. Use heat sinks for currents above 3A.

faqs.question: What voltage rating do I need for my bridge rectifier?
faqs.answer: Bridge rectifier voltage rating depends on input voltage: For 115VAC input: Use 400-600V bridges. Peak voltage is 115V × √2 = 163V, plus margin for line transients. For 230VAC or universal input (90-264VAC): Use 1000V bridges. Peak at 264V is 373V, plus margin for PFC boost if applicable. Key considerations: (1) Include 50-100% voltage margin for reliability; (2) PFC circuits may see higher voltages (400V DC bus); (3) Line transients can exceed nominal voltage; (4) Higher voltage bridges have slightly higher forward voltage. Panjit offers 600V bridges for 115V applications and 1000V bridges for universal input applications.
faqs.decisionGuide: Use 600V for 115V input, 1000V for 230V or universal input. Include margin for transients and PFC if applicable.

faqs.question: How do I handle inrush current with bridge rectifiers?
faqs.answer: Inrush current occurs at power-on when capacitors charge from zero voltage. This can be 10-50x normal current for a few milliseconds. Bridge rectifiers have IFSM (surge current) ratings for this: (1) Select bridge with IFSM rating higher than expected inrush; (2) Use NTC thermistors to limit inrush current; (3) Add series resistors or active current limit circuits; (4) Use soft-start circuits for large power supplies. Typical IFSM ratings: MB6S: 30A, GBU406: 120A, KBPC2510: 400A. For high-power supplies, consider phase-controlled soft-start or active PFC to eliminate inrush issues. Always verify inrush current with oscilloscope measurements during prototype testing.
faqs.decisionGuide: Select bridge with adequate IFSM rating. Consider inrush limiters for high-capacitance power supplies.

faqs.question: What is the difference between SMD and through-hole bridge rectifiers?
faqs.answer: SMD bridge rectifiers (MB series) offer: (1) Compact size for space-constrained designs; (2) Automated assembly compatibility; (3) Lower profile for slim designs; (4) Limited current capability (0.5-1A) due to thermal constraints; (5) Suitable for low-power adapters and LED drivers. Through-hole bridge rectifiers (GBU, KBPC series) offer: (1) Better thermal performance for higher currents; (2) Mechanical stability for heavy components; (3) Higher current capability (4-50A); (4) Chassis mounting options for high power; (5) Easier manual assembly and replacement. Selection depends on power level, thermal requirements, and assembly process. High-power applications (>10A) typically require through-hole or chassis-mount packages.
faqs.decisionGuide: Use SMD for low power (<2A) and space constraints. Use through-hole for higher power and better thermal performance.

faqs.question: How do I mount KBPC chassis-mount bridge rectifiers?
faqs.answer: KBPC chassis-mount bridge rectifiers require proper mounting for thermal performance: (1) Mounting surface - attach to metal chassis or heat sink using the threaded stud; (2) Thermal interface - use thermal compound or pad between bridge and mounting surface; (3) Torque - tighten to manufacturer specification (typically 0.8-1.2 Nm); (4) Isolation - use insulating washer if electrical isolation required; (5) Wire connections - use appropriate gauge wire for current rating. Thermal design: Calculate power dissipation P = 2 × VF × Idc. Ensure mounting surface can dissipate heat to maintain Tj < 150°C. For high-current applications, use forced air cooling or large heat sinks. Always verify temperature with thermocouple during testing.
faqs.decisionGuide: Mount to metal chassis or heat sink with thermal compound. Ensure adequate thermal capacity for power dissipation.

faqs.question: Can I parallel bridge rectifiers for higher current?
faqs.answer: Paralleling bridge rectifiers is generally not recommended due to current sharing issues. Unlike single diodes, bridge rectifiers have multiple diodes with variations in forward voltage that make current sharing unpredictable. Better alternatives: (1) Use single higher-current bridge (e.g., KBPC5010 instead of two KBPC2510s); (2) Use separate bridges for independent outputs; (3) Use Schottky output rectifiers after single bridge for higher current capability. If paralleling is necessary: (1) Use matched bridges from same production lot; (2) Add small series resistors (0.01-0.1 ohm) to improve sharing; (3) Monitor temperatures to detect imbalance; (4) Derate by 30-40% to account for uneven sharing. For most applications, selecting a single adequately-rated bridge is more reliable.
faqs.decisionGuide: Avoid paralleling bridges. Use single higher-current bridge or Schottky secondary rectifiers instead.

selectionGuide.title: How to Select TVS Diodes
selectionGuide.description: Learn about standoff voltage, clamping voltage, and power rating for effective circuit protection

faqs.question: How do I select the right standoff voltage for a TVS diode?
faqs.answer: Standoff voltage (Vrwm) is the maximum voltage the TVS can withstand in normal operation without conducting. Selection guidelines: (1) Vrwm must be higher than maximum normal operating voltage; (2) Include margin for voltage tolerances and transients; (3) For 5V circuits: use 5.0V or 6.0V TVS; (4) For 12V circuits: use 15V TVS; (5) For 24V circuits: use 24V or 27V TVS; (6) For 48V circuits: use 48V or 51V TVS. If Vrwm is too low, TVS will conduct during normal operation causing failure. If Vrwm is too high, clamping voltage may exceed protected circuit rating. Always check both Vrwm and Vc (clamping voltage) specifications.
faqs.decisionGuide: Select Vrwm above maximum normal voltage but ensure Vc is below circuit damage threshold.

faqs.question: What is clamping voltage and why is it important?
faqs.answer: Clamping voltage (Vc) is the maximum voltage across the TVS during a transient event when conducting peak pulse current. This is the voltage that your protected circuit will see during the surge. Critical considerations: (1) Vc must be below the damage threshold of protected components; (2) Check IC datasheets for absolute maximum voltage ratings; (3) Include safety margin - typically 10-20% below max rating; (4) Higher power TVS diodes generally have lower clamping voltage for same standoff voltage; (5) Bidirectional TVS have slightly higher Vc than unidirectional. Example: For protecting a 5V logic IC with 6V absolute max, select TVS with Vc < 5.5V at expected surge current.
faqs.decisionGuide: Ensure Vc is below your circuit's maximum voltage rating with safety margin.

faqs.question: What power rating TVS diode do I need?
faqs.answer: TVS power rating (PPPM) determines surge current capability: 400W (P4KE): Suitable for ESD protection and low-energy transients on signal lines. 600W (P6KE/SMBJ): General-purpose protection for power lines and I/O ports. 1500W (1.5KE/SMCJ): Higher surge capability for industrial and automotive applications. 5000W (5KP): Severe surge protection for load dump, lightning, and industrial transients. Selection depends on: (1) Expected transient energy; (2) Source impedance of transient; (3) Standards requirements (IEC, ISO); (4) PCB layout and trace inductance. When in doubt, use higher power rating for margin. Automotive applications typically require 1500W-5000W for load dump protection.
faqs.decisionGuide: Match TVS power rating to expected transient severity. Use higher rating for automotive and industrial applications.

faqs.question: Where should I place TVS diodes for best protection?
faqs.answer: TVS placement is critical for effective protection: (1) Place as close as possible to the connector or entry point - minimizes inductance between transient source and TVS; (2) Minimize trace length between TVS and protected line - reduces voltage overshoot due to trace inductance; (3) Use ground planes for low-impedance return path - reduces ground bounce during surge; (4) For differential pairs, place TVS across each line to ground and between lines; (5) Avoid vias between TVS and protected circuit if possible. Layout guidelines: Keep traces short and wide; Use Kelvin connections; Place TVS on same layer as protected traces when possible. Poor layout can reduce effective protection by 50% or more.
faqs.decisionGuide: Place TVS at connector with minimal trace length. Use good grounding practices.

faqs.question: What is the difference between unidirectional and bidirectional TVS?
faqs.answer: Unidirectional TVS: Conducts in reverse direction only; Suitable for DC circuits with known polarity; Lower clamping voltage for positive transients; Cathode connects to protected line, anode to ground. Bidirectional TVS: Conducts in both directions; Suitable for AC circuits or bipolar signals; Same clamping voltage for positive and negative transients; Can be used on any signal polarity. Selection: Use unidirectional for DC power rails (5V, 12V, 24V) for best protection. Use bidirectional for AC lines, data lines, and differential signals. In bidirectional TVS, two diodes are connected back-to-back, providing symmetrical protection. Clamping voltage is typically 10-15% higher than unidirectional for same standoff voltage.
faqs.decisionGuide: Use unidirectional for DC, bidirectional for AC and data lines. Unidirectional provides better protection for known polarities.

faqs.question: How do I protect against automotive load dump transients?
faqs.answer: Automotive load dump is a severe transient (ISO 7637-2 Pulse 5) caused by battery disconnect while alternator is charging. Characteristics: 12V system: up to 100V for 400ms; 24V system: up to 200V for 400ms; Source impedance: 0.5-4 ohms. Protection strategy: (1) Use 5000W TVS diodes (5KP series) for primary protection; (2) Place TVS at power entry point with short traces; (3) Use unidirectional TVS for DC lines; (4) Add series resistance or inductance to limit current; (5) Consider TVS + fuse combination for complete protection. TVS selection: 12V systems: 5KP22A or 5KP24A; 24V systems: 5KP36A or 5KP48A. Verify clamping voltage at expected surge current is below circuit maximum rating.
faqs.decisionGuide: Use 5000W TVS diodes for load dump protection. Place at power entry with good layout.
